title: Final - Gymnastics Project
text:
Our project focuses on data from major domestic and international gymnastics competitions from the 2022 and 2023 seasons.
For context on gymnastics terms, here is a useful guide to apparatus abbreviations. BB = Balanced Beam VT = Vault FX = Floor Exercise UB = Uneven Bars
Another helpful thing to keep in mind for gymnastics, is that Execution Score + Difficulty Score = Final Score. For this project, we’ll only be focusing on women’s scores. For a brief overview into the technical components of our projects we will: ● Use SQL and visualizations to identify the top 5 gymnasts who would optimize a team score (Fantasy Gymnastics!)  ● Use visualizations to explore difficulty vs execution tradeoffs to maximize score potential ● Use neural networks and statistical models to predict scores ● Analyze score distributions across athletes  ● Use Dash for users to view our visualizations  ● Use Dash, SQL, and visualizations for Monte Carlo Simulations

Our project focuses on the concept of Fantasy Gymnastics. We hoped to create a program that could identify the group of 5 athletes who will optimize success for the USA Olympic Women’s Artistic Gymnastics teams. We created an analytics model that can be used to identify and compare the expected medal count in 4 medal events for the women (vault, uneven bars, balance beam, and floor exercise). We created a Monte Carlo Simulation that uses a Mathematical technique with repeated random sampling to predict possible outcomes. We hope to run 1000 simulations where gymnasts compete against each other. We intend to use this to find the best-performing gymnasts that will make the team!
A consistent theme in this project is being able to filter to see a particular country’s results. By analyzing the score distributions across athletes and apparatuses, one can see different athlete’s weaknesses and strengths. We also utilized PyTorch to predict scores! This is helpful for gymnasts looking to improve their routines. We wanted our project to be useful to users which is why we incorporated a Dash App, which is user facing. We added features that users can use for a more interactive and helpful experience.

Pivoting using SQL
Our second function’s purpose is perform pivoting, meaning to transform the data from along form table to a wide form table. Achieving this will allow us to consolidate multiple rows of athlete’s scores across different events into just one row with the best scores of each event in each column.

By preparing the data in the right format, it will make it easier for us to perform Monte Carlo simulations, which will be described down in a later section of this blog post.

import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

from myProject import query_pivoted_database
print(inspect.getsource(query_pivoted_database)) 

pivoted_table = query_pivoted_database()
(pivoted_table)

def query_pivoted_database():
    """
    This function  connects to the SQL database to pivot it, meaning to transform the data from along form table to a wide form table. Achieving this will allow us to consolidate multiple rows of athlete’s scores across different events into just one row with the best scores of each event in each column. 

    Args:
        None

    Returns:
        df
    """
    with sqlite3.connect('gym') as conn: # connects to the SQL database to pivot it, meaning to transform the data from along form table to a wide form table. Achieving this will allow us to consolidate multiple rows of athlete’s scores across different events into just one row with the best scores of each event in each column. 

        cmd = f'''
        WITH AthleteScores AS (
            SELECT 
                LastName, 
                FirstName,
                Apparatus,
                AVG(Score) AS PredictedScore,
                COUNT(DISTINCT Date) AS CompetitionsCount,
                Country
            FROM gym 
            GROUP BY LastName, FirstName, Apparatus
        )
        SELECT 
            LastName, 
            FirstName,
            Country,
            MAX(CASE WHEN Apparatus = 'BB' THEN PredictedScore END) AS BB_PredictedScore,
            MAX(CASE WHEN Apparatus = 'VT' THEN PredictedScore END) AS VT_PredictedScore,
            MAX(CASE WHEN Apparatus = 'FX' THEN PredictedScore END) AS FX_PredictedScore,
            MAX(CASE WHEN Apparatus = 'UB' THEN PredictedScore END) AS UB_PredictedScore
          
        FROM AthleteScores
        GROUP BY LastName, FirstName, Country
        ORDER BY LastName, FirstName, Country
        '''

        df = pd.read_sql_query(cmd, conn)
    
    return df

def standardization(text):

    text = re.sub(f"[{string.punctuation}]", "", text)  #remove punctuation
    text = " ".join(word for word in text.split() if word not in stop_words) #remove stop words
    return text

def make_dataset(df):
    df["title"] = df["title"].apply(standardization) #apply to title

Implementation of parse_full_credits(self, response)
This method yields a scrapy.Request for the page of each actor listed on the page. This method works by obtaining the ordered list of crew by using response.css("ol.people.credits"). To get just the actors/cast, we index the 0th element because that’s the first section. Within each list, we enter the div called “info” and obtain the link. With this link, we append it to the base url and call the parse_actor_page(self,response), by specifying this method in the callback argument to a yielded scrapy.Request. We do this for all the links using list comprehension that is applied to the array of actor links.

import inspect
from TMDB_scraper.TMDB_scraper.spiders.tmdb_spider import TmdbSpider
print(inspect.getsource(TmdbSpider.parse_full_credits)) 

    def parse_full_credits(self, response):
        '''
        This method yields a scrapy.Request for the page of each actor listed on the page

        Args: response
        Yields: Request (naviation to each actor page)
        Returns: NA (this method does not return any data)
        
        The yielded request should specify the method parse_actor_page(self, response) should be called when the actor’s page is reached. 
        We obtain the ordered list of crew. To get just the actors/cast, we index the 0th element because that's the first section. 
        Within each list, we enter the div called "info" and obtain the link. With this link, we append it to the base url and 
        call the parse_actor_page(self,response), by specifying this method in the 
        callback argument to a yielded scrapy.Request. 
        '''       
        links = []
        actors = response.css("ol.people.credits")[0] #obtains the ordered list of crew. we index the 0th element to obtain just the actors/cast
        links = (actors.css("li div.info a::attr(href)").getall())   ## obtain a link associated with each actor
        yield from [scrapy.Request(url="https://www.themoviedb.org" + link, callback=self.parse_actor_page) for link in links]  #callback to the method parse_actor_page by using yielded scrapy.Request

                    yield { #dictionary with two key-value pairs, of the form {"actor" : actor_name, "movie_or_TV_name" : movie_or_TV_name}

To create our model with data augmentation, we use a model very identical to model1 but with some small adjustments and we add two new layers to this model at the very top called layers.RandomFlip("horizontal") and layers.RandomRotation(0.2). from tensorflow import keras

Data pre-processing
For this model, we will use data pre-processing which is when we handle the scaling so that the RGB values are normalized between 0 and 1, or -1 and 1. By scaling as the first step of the training process, we don’t have to waste energy adjusting the weights to the data scale later on. To do include this into our model, we add in the following code as the first layer that will create a preprocessing layer called preprocessor. We also add in our data augmentation layers from before.

i = keras.Input(shape=(150, 150, 3))
# The pixel values have the range of (0, 255), but many models will work better if rescaled to (-1, 1.)
# outputs: `(inputs * scale) + offset`
scale_layer = keras.layers.Rescaling(scale=1 / 127.5, offset=-1)
x = scale_layer(i)
preprocessor = keras.Model(inputs = i, outputs = x)

Sparse matrix in JAX
We can try making it faster! We can do so using sparse matrix data structures. The JAX package holds an experimental sparse matrix support. We can do this by using the batched coordinate (BCOO) format to only use O(n^2) space for the matrix, and only take O(n^2) time for each update, which is more efficient. It’s important we use the import from jax.experimental.sparse import BCOO, and ensure that the parameter is a jnp.array.

import inspect

print(inspect.getsource(get_sparse_A)) 

def get_sparse_A(N):
    """Creates matrix A using sparse matrix data structures
    Args:
        N: size of matrix A will be N^2 x N^2. 

    Returns:
        matrix A in a sparse format
    """
    n = N * N
    diagonals = [-4 * np.ones(n), np.ones(n-1), np.ones(n-1), np.ones(n-N), np.ones(n-N)]
    diagonals[1][(N-1)::N] = 0
    diagonals[2][(N-1)::N] = 0
    A = np.diag(diagonals[0]) + np.diag(diagonals[1], 1) + np.diag(diagonals[2], -1) + np.diag(diagonals[3], N) + np.diag(diagonals[4], -N)
    A_sp_matrix = BCOO.fromdense(jnp.array(A))
    return A_sp_matrix

text:
Direct operation with numpy
Let’s make it even more faster! We can do so by using vectorized array operations like np.roll() to advance the simulation by one timestep. The first thing we’ll need to do is padded = np.pad(u, 1, mode='constant'), which will help us pad zeroes to the input array to form a (N + 2) x (N + 2) array. This is important because one layer of padding is added to all edges of the array, which will help prevent out of bound errors with doing the vectorized array operations. The purpose of rolling it is to access the neighbors, which is needed for computation of the next timestep simulation. For np.roll, we accept the parameter of the newly padded variable, as well as the direction we’re moving it, and whether it’s up/down or right/left, which will help us get the surrounding neighbors.

import inspect
from heat_equation import advance_time_numpy
print(inspect.getsource(advance_time_numpy)) 

def advance_time_numpy(u, epsilon):
    """Advances the simulation by one timestep, via vectorized array operations like np.roll()
    Args:
        u: N x N grid state at timestep k.
        epsilon: stability constant.

    Returns:
        N x N Grid state at timestep k+1.
    """
    padded = np.pad(u, 1, mode='constant') #pad zeroes to the input array to form a (N + 2) x (N + 2) array
    ans = u + epsilon * (
        np.roll(padded, 1, axis=0)[1:-1, 1:-1] + #axis is 0 so moving values downward. the indexing after helps us remove the extra padding
        np.roll(padded, -1, axis=0)[1:-1, 1:-1] + #axis is 0 so moving values upward. the indexing after helps us remove the extra padding
        np.roll(padded, 1, axis=1)[1:-1, 1:-1] + #axis is 1 so moving values to the right. the indexing after helps us remove the extra padding
        np.roll(padded, -1, axis=1)[1:-1, 1:-1] - #axis is 1 so moving values to the left. the indexing after helps us remove the extra padding
        4 * u
    )
    return ans

Direct operation with jax using just-in-time compilation
Can we make it even more faster! Yes, with jax using just-in-time compilation! The first thing to do is add the line @jax.jit before we define the new function. We’ll have to do the same padding index as we did for numpy by doing padded = np.pad(u, 1, mode='constant'), which will help us pad zeroes to the input array to form a (N + 2) x (N + 2) array. This is important because one layer of padding is added to all edges of the array, which will help prevent out of bound errors with doing the vectorized array operations. Because jax does not support index assignment, we need to use direct array slicing, like this example u_padded[1:-1, 2:] that will help us get the right neighbor.

@jax.jit
def advance_time_jax(u, epsilon):
    """Advances the simulation by one timestep, via matrix-vector multiplication
    Args:
        u: N x N grid state at timestep k.
        epsilon: stability constant.

    Returns:
        N x N Grid state at timestep k+1.
    """
    u_padded = jnp.pad(u, pad_width=1, mode='constant')
    
    ans = u + epsilon * (
        u_padded[1:-1, 2:] +  #direct array slicing to get right neighbor
        u_padded[1:-1, :-2] +  #direct array slicing to get left neighbor
        u_padded[2:, 1:-1] +  #direct array slicing to get down neighbor
        u_padded[:-2, 1:-1] -  #direct array slicing to get up neighbor
        4 * u 
    )
    
    return ans

def query_climate_database( db_file, country, year_begin, year_end, month):

            Year: The year in which the reading was taken.

def query_climate_polars( db_file, country, year_begin, year_end, month):
    """Makes SQL query and outputs the data based on specific arguments

    Args:
        db_file (db): the file name for the database
        country (string): the name of a country for which data should be returned.
        year_begin (int):  the earliest years for which should be returned (inclusive).
        year_end (int): the latest years for which should be returned (inclusive).
        month (int): the month of the year for which should be returned.

    Returns:
        a Pandas dataframe of temperature readings for the specified country, 
        in the specified date range, in the specified month of the year. 
        This dataframe should have the following columns, in this order:

            NAME: The station name.
            LATITUDE: The latitude of the station.
            LONGITUDE: The longitude of the station.
            Country: The name of the country in which the station is located.
            Year: The year in which the reading was taken.
            Month: The month in which the reading was taken.
            Temp: The average temperature at the specified station during the specified year and month.
    """
    with sqlite3.connect(db_file) as conn:
        cmd = \
        f'''
        SELECT
        stations.name, latitude, longitude, countries.name as Country, year, month, temp  FROM temperatures
        INNER JOIN  stations on temperatures.ID = stations.ID --merging stations and temperatures 
        INNER JOIN countries ON SUBSTR(stations.ID, 1, 2) = countries."FIPS 10-4" --merging countries and temperatures 
        WHERE year >= {year_begin} AND year <= {year_end} AND month == {month}  AND countries.Name = '{country}'
        ORDER BY stations.name, year
        
        '''
        df = pl.read_database(cmd, conn) #using polars to read database and execute command
    return (df)

def one_more_query(db_file, station_name_one,station_name_two, temp_begin, temp_end ):

    Args:
        db_file (db): the file name for the database
        station_name_one (string): the name of a station for which data should be returned.
        station_name_two (string): the name of a second station for which data should be returned.
        temp_begin (int):  the lowest temps for which should be returned (inclusive).
        temp_end (int): the highest temps for which should be returned (inclusive).

        a Pandas dataframe of temperature readings for the specified country, 
        in the specified date range, in the specified month of the year. 
        This dataframe should have the following columns, in this order:

            NAME: The station name.
            Country: The name of the country in which the station is located.
            Year: The year in which the reading was taken.
            Month: The month in which the reading was taken.
            Temp: The average temperature at the specified station during the specified year and month.
            STNELEV: the standard elevation at the specific station
    """
    with sqlite3.connect(db_file) as conn:
        cmd = \
        f'''
        SELECT
        stations.name, countries.name as Country, year, month, temp, stations.STNELEV  FROM temperatures
        INNER JOIN  stations on temperatures.ID = stations.ID --merging stations and temperatures 
        INNER JOIN countries ON SUBSTR(stations.ID, 1, 2) = countries."FIPS 10-4" --merging countries and temperatures 
        WHERE temp >= {temp_begin} AND temp <= {temp_end} AND (stations.name == '{station_name_one}' or stations.name == '{station_name_two}') 
        ORDER BY stations.name, year
        
        '''
